newsitem.title: UK: FEATURE - Eastern Europe TV markets push for local content.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Eastern Europe TV markets push for local content.

text.p: Television continues to be a strong growth market in Central and Eastern Europe, but an increasing push for locally-produced programmes is taking hold as markets mature.
"The trend has started in Eastern Europe," says Brian Sturgess, global media strategist with ING Barings bank.
He describes the trend toward local content as "an inevitable process in any market."

In fact, this year's annual television fair in the French resort town of Cannes highlighted the fact that an increasing preference for local content over American imports has been taking hold throughout Europe.

"There was very much a focus on the fact that the big television programmes in Western Europe are decreasingly relying on America and producing their own stuff," said Robert Montgomery, managing director of Kagan World Media, a London-based research group.
"Markets go through a curve," Montgomery said. "There will always be a demand for hot Hollywood product but demand for locally produced fare also seems to be developing."
GROWING DEMAND FOR DOMESTICALLY-PRODUCED PROGRAMMES
Broadcasters who fail to meet audience demand for locally produced programmes could be sorry.
"Domestically-produced programmes and dramas will always get a higher market share," Sturgess says. "Anyone who doesn't heed that is headed for disaster."
Cathy Branson, Eastern European research analyst for Kagan World Media, says the push for locally produced TV programming reflects cultural tastes.

"Since the collapse of communism they've been inundated with U.S. programming, which has been badly dubbed and not enjoyable to watch," Branson said. "The general feeling now is they just want their own programming."

In the initial years after the collapse of communism, the dull, grey, state-sponsored programming that had ruled the airwaves gave way to a slew of glitzy, American imports. In fact, the Czech Republic's TV Nova, the most successful commercial TV station in Central and Eastern Europe and the brainchild of American cosmetics heir Ronald Lauder, built its original success on a diet of American series such as "Baywatch," American films and local news programmes.

But these days Central European Media Enterprises Ltd, the company founded by Lauder and which is the parent company of TV Nova and a host of other television stations throughout emerging Europe, emphasises the role of local content.

"In order to become the favourite television channel in one of those countries you have to be able to have a substantial amount of localism," CME chief executive Len Fertig told Reuters. "We try to get as close to 50 percent of all the programmes on those channels made in that country. They're either films or classic libraries that exist in those countries or their own film histories, in addition to (TV) shows actually created there."
TV Nova's schedule now includes nearly 50 percent Czech programming. The station's share of the Czech television audience has been running between 65 and 70 percent.
The challenge, however, is to produce programmes that rival the quality of Western imports.
Branson, of Kagan World Media, noted that for companies like CME it is cheaper to import American soap operas and serials rather than produce new programming.
"I think they would hope to increase local programming," she said. "The problem is a lot of local programming is bad."
In addition, she added, "because there is so little money being made in Eastern Europe at the moment, it's very hard to put money into programming."
GOVERNMENT QUOTAS

The push for local content, however, cannot be ignored, because governments increasingly are imposing quotas. Poland established a 30-percent minimum quota for locally produced programmes two years ago and has been strictly enforcing it.

Romania requires that 40 percent of television programmes be locally produced. Russia is discussing imposing a 20 percent local content quota -- although that may pose problems for local broadcasters whose tight economics force them to choose between importing high-quality programming from the West or offering low-quality, local content, Branson said.
Bulgaria is also discussing establishing a quota and Slovenia imposes a 10-percent quota.
CONTINUED GROWTH

In the meantime, however, television markets in emerging Europe are set for continued growth. Hungary is preparing to grant licences for two, new commercial stations in its first foray into commercial television.
"Hungary has enormous potential," said Sturgess of ING Barings. "You should see some rapid growth."

Zenith Media, a part of Cordiant Plc, the marketing and advertising group, says television advertising expenditure in Hungary shot up by 106 percent in 1996 to $188 million from $91 million in 1995. Zenith projects the market will grow 13 percent in 1997 and by 14.8 percent in 1998.

For the Czech Republic, Zenith sees a 23.1 percent increase in advertising expenditure for 1996 to $133 million from $108 million in 1995, and forecasts growth of nine percent in 1997 and 7.6 percent in 1998.

In Poland the television advertising market soared by 53.1 percent in 1996 to $512 million, and will rise another 24.8 percent in 1997 and 19.0 percent in 1998, according to Zenith. For Russia, TV adspend grew a healthy 15.1 percent to $649 million, is rising another 35 percent in 1997 and is expected to increase by 28.9 percent next year.

Overall, said Sturgess, "The (television) advertising markets are growing quite rapidly." The birth of new channels increases the amount of airtime available to advertisers and drives down advertising rates, and results in a wider range of advertisers using the medium.

That pattern will continue to protect television markets in emerging Europe from overall economic downturns, said Sturgess. "In Eastern Europe, even if GDP (gross domestic product) slows, you still have structural growth (in TV)," he says.
